strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem setting: unifying monocular video and multi-view capture in a single feed-forward 3DGS avatar reconstruction model with variable-length input is a genuine gap in the literature (LAM is single-frame, Ava3r is fixed 4-frame).

The incremental/streaming reconstruction capability is a novel and practically useful contribution, enabled by the Landmark Tracking Loss and Sliced Fusion Loss, and is demonstrated convincingly (Figure 5, Figure 11, streaming sliding-window experiments).

Comprehensive evaluation: comparisons across 1/4/8/16-view settings on NeRSemble and held-out subjects from Ava256, additional qualitative comparisons on INSTA and real-world data, and cross-reenactment results.

Solid ablation study (Table 2, Figure 9) covering each proposed component (sliced fusion loss, tracking loss, global attention, GS fusion, GS pruning), plus a thoughtful robustness study w.r.t. FLAME tracking noise (Table 4).
Strong quantitative gains over both feed-forward baselines (LAM) and optimization-based methods (GaussianAvatars, MonoGaussianAvatar), with favorable quality-speed trade-off in the 1-8 view regimes.
Ethics statement and detailed reproducibility appendix (hyperparameters, data preparation, FramePack design, training compute) are provided.
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: the method is largely an adaptation of VGGT to the avatar domain (replacing DPT with an MLP head, FLAME vertex positional prompts), combined with existing techniques (alternating attention from DiT, LAM initialization, LP-3DGS/MaskGaussian pruning, FramePack-style token compression). The contribution reads more as careful engineering than a fundamental methodological advance.

The 'fast' framing is somewhat overstated: FastAvatar is actually slower than LAM in modeling time (1.33s vs 0.31s at 1 view; 26.06s vs 0.69s at 16 views) and has lower rendering FPS at 8/16 views; its speed advantage holds only relative to optimization-based methods.

Comparison with Ava3r (the closest multi-view feed-forward baseline) is purely qualitative (Figure 6) using numbers taken from the Ava3r paper, with no quantitative table under a common protocol; the fairness of modifying LAM's renderer to fuse multi-frame inputs ('LAM*') is debatable and only partially justified.

Heavy dependence on FLAME/LBS anchoring is acknowledged as a limitation (no tongue, limited fine-grained dynamics, eye-gaze artifacts), which restricts fidelity compared to recent non-rigged gaussian avatar approaches; this ceiling is intrinsic to the method design.

Writing and notation issues: the fusion operator U(.) is underspecified (Eq. 3), the 'Identity' metric direction is confusing (lower-is-better is unusual for ArcFace similarity and requires careful reader interpretation), and there are several typos and awkward phrasings; Table 1 bold/underline conventions are not explained.
Code and models are only promised upon acceptance, which limits immediate reproducibility, although the appendix details are reasonably thorough.

strengths: Addresses a practically meaningful problem: unified, variable-length, incremental feed-forward 3D head avatar reconstruction from arbitrary numbers of monocular or multi-view frames, which existing fixed-input methods (LAM, Ava3r, optimization-based methods) cannot handle.

Reasonably comprehensive experimental protocol: comparisons across 1/4/8/16 input views against LAM, MonoGaussianAvatar, GaussianAvatars, and Ava3r (on Ava256), plus ablations of each proposed component, landmark-noise robustness, wide-viewpoint generalization, and streaming incremental reconstruction.

Good engineering integration: combining VGGT-style alternating global/frame attention, FLAME-anchored 3D positional prompts, sliced fusion loss, landmark tracking loss, and FramePack-style token compression is a coherent design, and the ablation table (Table 2) supports that each component contributes.

Strong speed and quality trade-off on sparse inputs (e.g., 20.08 PSNR at 1.33s for 1-view; 240 FPS rendering), and the appendix contains useful details (hyperparameters, data preparation, FramePack formulation, failure cases).
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the method is largely an adaptation of existing components to the avatar domain — VGGT's architecture (replacing DPT with an MLP), DINOv2 features, LAM's frame-attention initialization, FLAME/LBS anchoring as in GaussianAvatars, FramePack token compression, and LP-3DGS/MaskGaussian pruning. The individual contributions (sliced fusion loss, landmark tracking loss) are relatively straightforward, and the paper does not clearly articulate a fundamentally new insight beyond 'aggregate per-frame Gaussians'.

The core fusion operator U(·) (Eq. 3) — the key mechanism for incremental reconstruction — is never precisely defined (is it learned attention, concatenation, averaging, point-cloud merging?), making the central contribution hard to assess and reproduce. Several other details (unordered token handling, how GS fusion avoids ghosting at inference) are similarly underspecified.

Speed claims are overstated: while 1-view reconstruction is fast, the modeling time grows to 8.56s (8 views) and 26.06s (16 views), and optimization-based baselines remain competitive in that regime; at 16 views FastAvatar is no longer clearly 'seconds-fast' relative to alternatives.

Evaluation has gaps: the main benchmark is self-constructed from NeRSemble (the training data source) rather than an established avatar benchmark; comparisons on NeRSemble-derived test sets risk train/test distribution overlap; quantitative results on INSTA/Ava256 are mostly qualitative or limited to headline LPIPS/Identity numbers; cross-identity metrics could favor FLAME-anchored methods.

Baselines are modified (LAM* altered to fuse multiple frames by the authors) without released code to verify fairness of these modifications; some claims (e.g., 'LAM degrades with more views') rely on the authors' own adapted variant.

Dependence on FLAME proxy and LBS limits representational capability (acknowledged), and the incremental quality gains with more views are modest in quantitative terms for the added modeling cost; the quality-speed 'paradigm' claim is not rigorously characterized (no explicit quality-speed Pareto analysis).

Writing quality is uneven: the introduction and methodology contain marketing-style language ('Extensive experiments', 'optimal equilibrium', 'pioneers'), and Figure 2 is dense and hard to parse, weakening clarity relative to a top-tier standard.

strengths: Clear and practical problem formulation: unifying single-image, monocular video, and multi-view few-shot avatar reconstruction in one feed-forward model, with variable-length input, which existing feed-forward methods (LAM, Ava3r) do not support.

The proposed LGRT design is reasonable and well-motivated: replacing VGGT's dense prediction transformer head with an MLP producing canonical 3DGS, using FLAME vertices as positional prompts, interleaved global/frame attention, and the Sliced Fusion Loss + Landmark Tracking Loss for consistent fusion of per-frame Gaussians.

Strong quantitative results across 1/4/8/16 view settings with competitive quality-speed trade-off (e.g., 240 FPS rendering at 1 view, seconds-scale modeling time), plus ablations (Table 2) covering each claimed component, robustness to FLAME landmark noise (Table 4), and evaluation on a held-out dataset (Ava256) for the multi-view task.
Honest limitations section (FLAME/LBS dependence, tongue and eye-gaze failure modes), ethics and reproducibility statements, and detailed hyperparameters in the appendix.

Incremental/streaming reconstruction is a genuinely new capability for feed-forward avatar models, demonstrated qualitatively (Figures 4, 5, 11) and supported by the FramePack-style token compression design.
weaknesses: The 'incremental reconstruction' claim is softer than marketed. In the main setting the model still ingests all frames jointly; 'incrementality' largely amounts to variable-length input plus a sliding-window/FramePack extension described only briefly in the appendix (C.3), which lacks quantitative evaluation. True streaming consistency (e.g., drift accumulation over long windows) is not rigorously measured.

Training and the main evaluation are both on NeRSemble (with train/test subject splits, but the same capture rig and 12-camera distribution). Cross-dataset generalization is only shown qualitatively (INSTA in Fig. 7) without a full quantitative cross-domain benchmark, so claims about 'daily recordings' and in-the-wild robustness are not strongly supported.

Baseline fairness concerns: LAM is modified by the authors (LAM*, with a custom multi-frame fusing renderer) rather than evaluated as released, and some comparison numbers rely on results reported in another paper (Ava3r on Ava256). The modified renderer could disadvantage the baseline.

Identity metric behavior is unexplained: LAM's Identity scores (e.g., 0.299 at 4 views vs. FastAvatar 0.098) are much worse than its visual quality suggests, and the paper attributes this to 'pose and expression artifacts' without analysis; conversely, lower Identity scores for the proposed method are reported as better without validating the metric direction.

Dependence on FLAME tracking at both training and inference (with expression/pose coefficients from external tracking) limits applicability to non-face-topology content and makes the pipeline partially optimization-based in preprocessing, somewhat weakening the 'feed-forward in seconds' framing.

The FramePack extension (which enables the headline 512-frame results and OOM avoidance) is underdeveloped in the main text: no ablation on the compression rate, no quantitative comparison of streamed vs. joint reconstruction quality.

No comparison against recent feed-forward Gaussian reconstruction methods adapted to heads (e.g., AnySplat/NoPoS-style), and no user study, so perceptual superiority beyond PSNR/LPIPS is not established.
